children: By Sharon Kimathi

Today's newsletter focuses on the environment and governance themes that will be addressed at the 2026 UN General Assembly, which takes place against a backdrop of rising temperatures, geopolitical tension over minerals and the rise of AI.

US President Donald Trump is expected to kick it off with a speech. Last year, he told delegates that some countries were "going to hell" for, among other things, ⁠climate policy and mass migration. Click here for the latest on who he is meeting.
This year’s General Assembly faces an existential debate over the UN’s relevance, with the theme: "Restoring trust, managing transformation: A United Nations that delivers for all”.
UN RELEVANCE IN ADDRESSING CRISES
The UN is struggling to remain relevant as it
, whose administration has cut US contributions and withdrawn from dozens of UN bodies.

The US avoided losing its vote at the assembly ​by paying $725 million in contributions to the regular budget last week, but it still owes the UN more than $1 billion and makes ongoing demands for cuts and reforms.

Additionally, China’s President Xi Jinping, who last addressed the meeting via video in 2021, will skip New York in favour of talks with Trump in Washington on Thursday, adding to the debate about the UN's relevance in addressing global crises.

There are also questions about the leadership of the 80-year-old organization as Secretary-General Antonio Guterres completes his term at the end of 2026, with no clear frontrunner in the race ​to replace him.
Guterres told reporters ahead of the meeting that the need for stronger oversight would be a major ​focus of his talks with global leaders gathered in New York.
GREENLAND AND EXCEEDING 1.5 DEGREES CELSIUS

Trump is also due to meet with leaders ‌of Greenland and Denmark on Tuesday to sign a deal that will allow a larger US military presence on Greenland and could end a standoff over the strategically located and mineral-rich island.
Greenland, a former colony and now a semi-autonomous territory of the Kingdom of ​Denmark, sits between the Arctic and North America.

Climate change will also be on the agenda as the world struggles to limit warming to 1.5 degrees Celsius above pre-industrial levels. World leaders agreed to limit warming in ​the 2015 Paris climate agreement and heads of smaller island nations and other states most affected by climate change are expected to again urge action.
August was the first month since November 2025 in which the world's average temperature exceeded 1.5 C above pre-industrial levels.
TALKING POINTS

Tesla racism lawsuit: A lawsuit by the California Civil Rights Department, a state agency, accusing Tesla of allowing rampant race discrimination at its flagship assembly plant began trial this week and is scheduled to run until October 30. In the lawsuit filed in 2022, the agency claims Black workers at Tesla's Fremont, California, plant were subjected to pervasive harassment by other employees, including racial slurs and graffiti, and Tesla failed to prevent or stop it. Tesla has denied wrongdoing. Click here to learn more about the suit.
Taxes and inequality: A ballot initiative on November 3 will ask Californians whether to impose a ‌one-time
. The proposition is far from certain to pass, political analysts say, amid a debate that has raised questions about income inequality and California’s future business prospects.

Cuba crisis: Cuba's electrical grid suffered a total collapse at the weekend, leaving millions without power amid a US pressure ‌campaign that has largely blocked oil from reaching the Caribbean's largest island. The latest of at least six partial or total grid collapses since January hardly registered in a ​country accustomed to long hours, or even days, without power.

Bangladesh factory cooling: Brands should share the cost burden when investing in cooling systems to reduce ‌heat stress for garment factory workers, researchers ​at Cornell University's Global Labor Institute said in a report, as climate change poses growing risks to apparel production hubs. Click here for the full Reuters insight.

New Zealand carbon credits: For almost 20 years, New Zealand has pioneered one of the world’s most ambitious tree-planting programs, approving nearly 9,000 square kilometers of carbon-credit forest. That’s about 11 times the land area of New York City. Yet the boom in carbon forestry, and tradable carbon credits, has also driven competition for sheep and beef farming land.

IN CONVERSATION
Kaysie Brown, associate director of climate diplomacy and geopolitics at climate change think tank E3G, shares her thoughts on the UN General Assembly:
"As the majority of the world's leaders come together in New York, this is the moment to stand fast on cooperation in a fragmenting world.

“The crises on their agenda, from energy shocks from ongoing conflict in the Middle East and Ukraine to record heat, wildfires and a looming El Niño, are not reasons to set climate aside; they are the reason to act on it, faster and together.”

“In Secretary-General Guterres's final year, leaders must show their resolve in building on the economic opportunities that clean energy and climate action affords, and to tackle challenges jointly to build the resilience their people need."
